records.original_statement:
Let $U\subset\R^n$ be open and $f\colon U\to\R^m$. The map $f$ is \emph{differentiable at $a\in U$} if there is a linear map $Df(a)\colon\R^n\to\R^m$
with
\[
f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+o(|h|)\qquad(h\to0).
\]
It is \emph{$C^1$} if it is differentiable at every point and $a\mapsto Df(a)$ is continuous, $C^k$ if moreover $Df$ is $C^{k-1}$, and \emph{smooth}
($C^\infty$) if it is $C^k$ for every $k$.

\]
Composing $C^k$ maps gives a $C^k$ map.

\[
\varphi(M\cap U)=V\cap(\R^k\times\{0\}).
\]

records.original_statement:
\label{thm:fourdesc}
Let $M\subset\R^N$, $p\in M$ and $0\le k\le N$. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{Straightening:} there is a diffeomorphism $\varphi\colon U\to V$ between open sets of $\R^N$, with $p\in U$ and
$\varphi(M\cap U)=V\cap(\R^k\times\{0\})$.
\item \emph{Equations:} there are an open $U\ni p$ and a smooth $F\colon U\to\R^{N-k}$ with $M\cap U=F^{-1}(0)$ and $DF(x)$ surjective for every
$x\in M\cap U$.
\item \emph{Graph:} after a permutation of the coordinates of $\R^N=\R^k\times\R^{N-k}$, there are open sets $\Omega\subset\R^k$ and $B\subset\R^{N-k}$ with
$p\in\Omega\times B$, and a smooth $g\colon\Omega\to B$, such that $M\cap(\Omega\times B)$ is the graph of $g$.
\item \emph{Parametrization:} there are an open $\Omega\subset\R^k$, an open $U\ni p$ and a smooth $\psi\colon\Omega\to\R^N$ such that $\psi$ is injective,
$D\psi(x)$ is injective for every $x$, $\psi(\Omega)=M\cap U$, and $\psi$ is a homeomorphism from $\Omega$ onto $M\cap U$.
\end{enumerate}
So $M$ is a $k$-dimensional submanifold if and only if one of them holds at every point of $M$.
records.current_statement:
\label{thm:fourdesc}
For $p\in M\subset\R^N$ and $0\le k\le N$, the following local descriptions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{Straightening.} A diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to V$ of ambient open sets, with $p\in U$, satisfies $\varphi(M\cap U)=V\cap(\R^k\times\{0\})$.
\item \emph{Equations.} On some open $U\ni p$ there is a smooth $F:U\to\R^{N-k}$ with $M\cap U=F^{-1}(0)$ and $DF(x)$ surjective at every $x\in M\cap U$.
\item \emph{Graph.} After permuting ambient coordinates, there are open $\Omega\subset\R^k$, $B\subset\R^{N-k}$ and smooth $g:\Omega\to B$ such that $p\in\Omega\times B$ and $M\cap(\Omega\times B)=\{(x,g(x)):x\in\Omega\}$.
\item \emph{Parametrization.} There are open $\Omega\subset\R^k$, ambient open $U\ni p$, and smooth $\psi:\Omega\to\R^N$ such that $\psi$ is injective, each $D\psi(x)$ is injective, its image is $M\cap U$, and $\psi:\Omega\to M\cap U$ is a homeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently any one of these descriptions at every point characterizes a $k$-dimensional submanifold.

records.original_statement:
\label{ex:on}
Let $\mathrm{Sym}_n$ be the space of symmetric $n\times n$ matrices, of dimension $\frac{n(n+1)}2$, and $F\colon M_n(\R)\to\mathrm{Sym}_n$,
$F(X)=X^\top X-I$, so that $\mathrm O(n)=F^{-1}(0)$. Expanding $F(X+H)$ gives
\[
DF(X)H=H^\top X+X^\top H.
\]
If $X\in\mathrm O(n)$ and $S\in\mathrm{Sym}_n$, then $H=\frac12XS$ satisfies $H^\top X=\frac12SX^\top X=\frac12S$ and $X^\top H=\frac12S$, so
$DF(X)H=S$: the derivative is surjective onto $\mathrm{Sym}_n$. By (b), $\mathrm O(n)$ is a submanifold of $M_n(\R)=\R^{n^2}$ of dimension
\[
n^2-\tfrac{n(n+1)}2=\tfrac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
It is compact, being closed and bounded (each column is a unit vector). The determinant is $\pm1$ on $\mathrm O(n)$, so $\mathrm{SO}(n)=\mathrm O(n)\cap\{\det>0\}$
is open in $\mathrm O(n)$, hence also a submanifold of dimension $\frac{n(n-1)}2$. For $n=2$ this is a circle; for $n=3$ it is three-dimensional, which
matches the count ``an axis (two parameters) and an angle (one)''.

records.original_statement:
\label{ex:cassini}
Let $f(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^2-2(x^2-y^2)$. Writing $z=x+iy$ one checks $f=|z-1|^2|z+1|^2-1$, so the level set $f=c$ is the set of points whose distances to
$\pm1$ have product $\sqrt{1+c}$: a Cassini oval. The gradient is
\[
\nabla f=\bigl(4x(x^2+y^2-1),\ 4y(x^2+y^2+1)\bigr),
\]
which vanishes only at $(0,0)$ and $(\pm1,0)$, with values $0$ and $-1$. So every level $c>-1$ other than $0$ is a curve, by (b); for
$-1<c<0$ it has two components, for $c>0$ one (Figure~\ref{fig:cassini}). The level $0$ is Jacob Bernoulli's lemniscate, a figure eight, which is not a
submanifold at the origin; the level $-1$ is the two points $(\pm1,0)$, which \emph{is} a $0$-dimensional submanifold: the condition in (b) is
sufficient, not necessary.
records.current_statement:
\label{ex:cassini}
For
\[
f(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^2-2(x^2-y^2)=|z-1|^2|z+1|^2-1,
\]
the level $f=c$ fixes the product of distances to $\pm1$ at $\sqrt{1+c}$ when $c\ge-1$. Its gradient is
\[
\nabla f=(4x(x^2+y^2-1),\ 4y(x^2+y^2+1)).
\]
It vanishes only at $0$ and $(\pm1,0)$, with respective values $0,-1,-1$. Every nonempty level with $c>-1$, $c\ne0$, is therefore a smooth curve.

Polar coordinates give the component count: for $u=x^2+y^2>0$, the equation is $u^2-2u\cos2\theta=c$. If $c>0$, exactly one root is positive for every angle, giving one oval. If $-1<c<0$, positive roots exist in two angular intervals about the positive and negative horizontal axes; the two radial roots meet at each interval's ends, giving two ovals. At $c=0$ the branches form Bernoulli's crossing lemniscate, which is not a smooth submanifold at the crossing. At $c=-1$ only $(\pm1,0)$ remain, a zero-dimensional submanifold; below $-1$ the level is empty. A vanishing derivative of one defining function does not rule out a manifold: description (b) asks for the existence of a suitable defining function.

records.original_statement:
A \emph{topological manifold of dimension $n$} is a topological space $M$ that is Hausdorff, has a countable basis of open sets, and in which every point
has an open neighbourhood $U$ homeomorphic to an open subset of $\R^n$. Such a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon U\to\varphi(U)\subset\R^n$ is a
\emph{chart}. Two charts $(U,\varphi)$, $(U',\varphi')$ are \emph{compatible} if the \emph{transition map}
\[
\varphi'\circ\varphi^{-1}\colon\varphi(U\cap U')\to\varphi'(U\cap U')
\]
is smooth, and so is its inverse $\varphi\circ\varphi'^{-1}$. An \emph{atlas} is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $M$.

restriction to $M$ of a smooth map defined on an open set of $\R^N$ is smooth.

records.original_statement:
\label{ex:rpn}
Let $\R P^n$ be the set of lines through $0$ in $\R^{n+1}$, the quotient of $\R^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ by $x\sim\lambda x$ ($\lambda\ne0$), with the quotient
topology; write $[x]=[x_0:\dots:x_n]$. The quotient map $\pi$ is open, because $\pi^{-1}(\pi(O))=\bigcup_{\lambda\ne0}\lambda O$ is open when $O$ is.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Charts.} On the open set $U_i=\{[x]:x_i\ne0\}$ let $\varphi_i([x])=\bigl(\frac{x_j}{x_i}\bigr)_{j\ne i}\in\R^n$. It is a homeomorphism onto
$\R^n$, with inverse $u\mapsto[u_0:\dots:1:\dots:u_n]$ ($1$ in position $i$). On $\varphi_i(U_i\cap U_j)$ the transition map $\varphi_j\circ\varphi_i^{-1}$
divides every coordinate by $u_j\ne0$, after inserting a $1$ in position $i$: it is smooth.
\item \emph{Countable basis.} $\R P^n$ is the union of $n+1$ open sets homeomorphic to $\R^n$.
\item \emph{Hausdorff.} The map $P([x])=\frac{xx^\top}{|x|^2}$ is well defined and continuous on $\R P^n$, with values in the matrices. It is injective,
because $P([x])$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line $\R x$, which determines the line. Two points with distinct images under a continuous
injective map into a Hausdorff space have disjoint neighbourhoods.
\end{itemize}
Moreover $\R P^n=\pi(S^n)$ is compact.
records.current_statement:
\label{ex:rpn}
The real projective space $\R P^n$ consists of lines in $\R^{n+1}$, with $[x]=[x_0:\cdots:x_n]$ identifying $x$ and $\lambda x$ for $\lambda\ne0$. Give it the quotient topology from $\R^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$. The quotient map $\pi$ is open, since $\pi^{-1}\pi(O)=\bigcup_{\lambda\ne0}\lambda O$ is open for open $O$.

On $U_i=\{[x]:x_i\ne0\}$ define $\varphi_i([x])=(x_j/x_i)_{j\ne i}$. This is a homeomorphism to $\R^n$: its inverse inserts $1$ in position $i$ and applies the quotient map, while its forward continuity follows from the quotient property. To change from chart $i$ to chart $j$, divide the inserted coordinate list by its nonzero $j$th coordinate and omit that coordinate. These rational expressions and their inverses are smooth.

The $n+1$ chart domains give a countable basis. To check Hausdorffness, use the continuous map
\[
[x]\longmapsto\frac{xx^\top}{|x|^2}.
\]
It is injective because its matrix is the orthogonal projection onto the line $\R x$. Distinct image matrices have disjoint neighbourhoods, whose inverse images separate the original points. Thus $\R P^n$ is a smooth $n$-manifold. It is compact, being the image of $S^n$ under $\pi$; for $n=0$ it is one point.

\label{prop:tangentsub}
Let $M\subset\R^N$ be a $k$-dimensional submanifold and $p\in M$. Let $T_pM$ be the set of velocities $\gamma'(0)$ of smooth curves
$\gamma\colon\left]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\right[\to\R^N$ with values in $M$ and $\gamma(0)=p$. For any $F$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:fourdesc}(b) and any $\psi$
as in (d) with $\psi(x_0)=p$,
\[
T_pM=\operatorname{im}D\psi(x_0)=\ker DF(p).
\]
In particular $T_pM$ is a $k$-dimensional vector space, and $k$ is determined by $M$.

\]
Such maps, also called derivations at $p$, form the vector space $T_pM$.

\[a_1b_1a_1^{-1}b_1^{-1}\cdots a_gb_ga_g^{-1}b_g^{-1}:\]

\[\pi_1(\Sigma_g)\cong\bigl\langle a_1,b_1,\dots,a_g,b_g\mid[a_1,b_1]\cdots[a_g,b_g]\bigr\rangle,\qquad[a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1},\]

non-isomorphic fundamental groups and are not homeomorphic, nor even homotopy equivalent. For $g=1$ we recover $\Z^2$. The projective plane is a disc with antipodal boundary points identified,

$f,g$ are \emph{chain homotopic} if there are $P\colon C_k\to C'_{k+1}$ with $\partial P+P\partial=g-f$; then $f_*=g_*$, because for a cycle $z$, $g(z)-f(z)=\partial P(z)$ is a boundary.

Example~\ref{ex:surfaces}, $V$ a small open disc in the polygon and $U$ the complement of its centre. Then $U$ deformation retracts onto the wedge of $2g$ circles, $V$ is contractible, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto a circle, whose generator maps in $H_1(U)$ to $h$ of the boundary word, $a_1+b_1-a_1-b_1+\dots=0$. Reduced Mayer--Vietoris reads
\[0\to H_2(\Sigma_g)\to H_1(S^1)=\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z^{2g}\to H_1(\Sigma_g)\to\tilde H_0(S^1)=0,\]
so $H_2(\Sigma_g)=\Z$, $H_1(\Sigma_g)=\Z^{2g}$, $H_0=\Z$, and $\chi(\Sigma_g)=2-2g$. This is the value of the index sum of Chapter~4 for the pretzel with $g$ holes, which is homeomorphic to
$\Sigma_g$ (this follows from the classification of surfaces, a remark here).

\label{ex:surfacesH}
\emph{Turning loops into homology classes.} A loop is a singular $1$-cycle. For based loops $\gamma,\eta$, compose $\gamma\eta$ with the affine map $\Delta^2\to I$ taking its vertices to $0,1/2,1$. Its boundary is $\eta-\gamma\eta+\gamma$. Thus concatenation becomes addition in $H_1$. A based homotopy gives a homology by the prism operator; its constant side paths cancel. We obtain a homomorphism $h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to H_1(X)$.

On $S^1$, cover by two open arcs with intersection two arcs. Mayer--Vietoris gives $H_1(S^1)\cong\tilde H_0(\text{two points})=\Z$. Subdividing a positive loop into its arc pieces sends it under $\delta$ to the difference of the two overlap components, a generator up to sign. Hence $h$ identifies the winding generator of $\pi_1(S^1)$ with a generator of $H_1(S^1)$. By naturality, a circle map's action on $H_1$ is multiplication by its winding number, so this is its degree.

\emph{Surface groups become abelian.} Use the bouquet open covers from Chapter~5 with Mayer--Vietoris. Their contractible star intersections show that a bouquet of $m$ circles has $H_1=\Z^m$, with its loops as generators, and all higher homology zero. For $\Sigma_g$, remove the polygon disc's centre to obtain $U$, retracting onto the bouquet of $2g$ circles, and take its open interior as $V$. The intersection retracts onto its boundary circle. The attaching word has homology class
\[
a_1+b_1-a_1-b_1+\cdots+a_g+b_g-a_g-b_g=0.
\]
Reduced Mayer--Vietoris therefore contains
\[
0\to H_2(\Sigma_g)\to\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z^{2g}
\to H_1(\Sigma_g)\to0.
\]
It follows that $H_2=\Z$, $H_1=\Z^{2g}$, $H_0=\Z$, and all higher groups vanish. Thus $\chi(\Sigma_g)=2-2g$. For $g=0$ the sphere computation gives the same formula directly. This is also the index sum found in Chapter~4 for a smooth surface with $g$ handles.

\label{thm:torus}
Let $T\subset U(n)$ be the diagonal unitary subgroup, isomorphic to
$(S^1)^n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Each element of $U(n)$ is conjugate by a unitary matrix to an
element of $T$. The exponential $\mathfrak u(n)\to U(n)$ is onto and
$U(n)$ is connected.
\item[(b)] If $t\in T$ has distinct diagonal entries, its centraliser in
$U(n)$ is exactly $T$. Consequently $T$ is maximal abelian.
\item[(c)] Its normaliser $N(T)=\{g\in U(n):gTg^{-1}=T\}$ consists
of the matrices $P_wD$, where $D\in T$ and $P_w$ is a permutation
matrix. The quotient $N(T)/T$ is $S_n$, acting by permuting diagonal entries.
\item[(d)] Two elements of $T$ are conjugate in $U(n)$ exactly when their
diagonal entries agree after a permutation.
\end{enumerate}

\label{ex:su2haar}
A matrix of $SU(2)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$, and is determined by its first column; this identifies $SU(2)$ with the unit sphere
$S^3\subset\C^2=\R^4$. Under this identification, left multiplication by $g\in SU(2)$ is the map $z\mapsto gz$ on first columns, which is unitary, hence an orthogonal map of $\R^4$.
The uniform probability $\sigma_3$ on $S^3$ is the law of $Z/|Z|$ for a standard Gaussian vector $Z$ in $\R^4$ (polar coordinates, as in the solution of Exercise~\ref{ex:spherevolume}), and
the Gaussian law is invariant under orthogonal maps. So $\sigma_3$ is a left invariant probability on $SU(2)$: \emph{the Haar measure of $SU(2)$ is the uniform measure on $S^3$.}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:pushhaar} and the double cover $SU(2)\to SO(3)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}, a Haar random rotation is obtained by taking a uniform point of $S^3$, a unit
quaternion, and the rotation it induces. This is how computer graphics draws random orientations (Ken Shoemake's method of 1992), and Exercise~\ref{ex:su2weyl} computes
how large the angle of a random rotation is.

\label{ex:su2haar}

map $z\mapsto gz$, hence by an orthogonal map of $\R^4$.
For a standard real Gaussian vector $Z\in\R^4$, polar coordinates show
that $Z/|Z|$ has uniform spherical probability, as in
Exercise~\ref{ex:spherevolume}. The zero vector has probability zero.
The Gaussian law and the spherical probability are invariant under all
orthogonal maps, so this spherical law is left invariant on $SU(2)$.
Uniqueness makes it Haar probability.

Push it through the spin covering of Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.
A uniform unit quaternion therefore produces a Haar random spatial
rotation. This is the basis of Shoemake's random-orientation construction.
It does not mean choosing the rotation angle uniformly: the angle density
will be computed in Exercise~\ref{ex:su2weyl}.

records.current_statement:
\label{thm:trace}
Let $g\in SL_2(\R)$ with $g\ne\pm I$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|<2$, then $g$ has exactly one fixed point $z_0\in\mathbb H$ and is conjugate to some $k_\theta$. It is a rotation about $z_0$, called \emph{elliptic}.
\item[(b)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|=2$, then $g$ has no fixed point in $\mathbb H$ and exactly one in $\R\cup\{\infty\}$. It is conjugate to $\pm n_1$ or $\pm n_{-1}$ and is called \emph{parabolic}.
\item[(c)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|>2$, then $g$ is conjugate to $\pm\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$, where $\lambda>1$, and is called \emph{hyperbolic}. It fixes two boundary points and translates their joining h-line, its \emph{axis}, by $\ell=2\log\lambda$. For every $z\in\mathbb H$,
\[
d(z,g(z))\ge\ell,
\qquad 2\cosh(\ell/2)=|\operatorname{tr}g|,
\]
with equality in the distance inequality exactly on the axis.
\end{enumerate}
